body:
With Alex entering a new chapter as a mom, we couldn't help imagining what her dream nursery might look like. Would it be all neutrals? A little unexpected? Effortlessly sophisticated with just enough personality?

If we had the chance to style it, we'd take inspiration from her home's warm textures, natural materials, and understated elegance, then add a few playful details that feel right for a baby's first room.

Of course, this is our own imagined design, not a reveal of Alex's actual nursery or a collaboration. But if you're looking for a celebrity-inspired nursery that feels grown-up without losing its charm, here's how we'd bring the look to life.

When Architectural Digest toured Alex Cooper's Los Angeles home, the interiors revealed a different side of the podcast star. Think earthy materials, natural light, warm wood, neutral colors, and layers of inviting textures.

The home was designed to feel comfortable and lived-in rather than overly formal. That's exactly the approach we'd take with a nursery.

Our imaginary Alex Cooper nursery would start with a simple palette:

  • Warm ivory and cream for the walls and larger surfaces.
  • Rich walnut wood to bring depth and warmth to the furniture.
  • Soft blush as an unexpected accent, inspired by the pink closet featured in her home tour.
  • Muted olive or sage green to connect the space with nature.
  • Textured fabrics to make the room feel cozy without needing lots of decoration.

The result? A nursery that feels sophisticated enough to belong in a beautifully designed home, but still warm and welcoming for a little one.

The Crib We'd Choose: The Bliss 4-in-1 in Walnut

Every great nursery needs a centerpiece, and we'd let the crib do the talking.

For this particular mood board, we'd choose the dadadababy Bliss 4-in-1 Convertible Crib in Walnut.

Handcrafted in Italy from solid European beechwood, the Bliss has clean, modern lines and a rich wood finish that would fit beautifully with the natural materials throughout Alex's home.

What makes it particularly appealing is that it isn't designed only for the newborn stage. The Bliss offers four configurations: crib, toddler bed, daybed, and floor bed, with applicable conversion components and instructions for each stage.

We love the idea of choosing a piece that can stay in the room as it evolves. A beautiful crib today could eventually become a little bed your toddler climbs into independently when they're ready and the manufacturer's requirements are met.

Before purchasing, we'd check the exact conversion instructions and required parts. The toddler-bed and daybed conversion kit is sold separately, so it's worth planning for that future purchase from the beginning.

Next, A Dresser That's Beautiful Enough to Stay

One thing we'd avoid? Filling the room with furniture that only works while the baby is in diapers.

For storage, we'd choose the Bliss 6-Drawer Nursery Dresser in White + Walnut.

Its combination of light and dark finishes would complement the walnut crib without making everything feel overly matched. The six drawers provide practical storage for baby clothes, blankets, and everyday essentials.

And here's where we'd get a little strategic: instead of adding a completely separate changing table, we'd consider the removable changing tray designed for compatible Bliss dressers.

During the newborn stage, the tray creates a dedicated changing station when correctly installed and used according to its instructions. Once diaper changes are behind you, it can be removed, leaving a dresser that still works beautifully in a toddler's bedroom.

That feels much more intentional than purchasing an entire piece of furniture you'll need to replace in a year or two.

We'd also secure the dresser to the wall using the manufacturer's specified anti-tip hardware before putting it into use.

The Details: Cozy, Personal, and Just a Little Playful

Here's where we'd have some fun.

Alex's home has plenty of sophisticated materials, but it doesn't feel like a place where you're afraid to touch anything. We'd bring that same energy into the nursery.

Imagine a comfortable upholstered chair in a soft, textured fabric, a beautiful woven rug, and a warm reading light for nighttime care.

Then we'd introduce something unexpected.

Maybe a playful art print. A vintage-inspired lamp safely positioned out of a child's reach. Or a small blush-colored detail that adds a little personality to an otherwise neutral room.

We wouldn't want every accessory to match perfectly. Mixing textures, shapes, and carefully chosen objects can make a room feel more personal.

And because a baby's nursery will eventually become a child's bedroom, we'd leave some space for that personality to develop naturally. There will be plenty of time for favorite books, toys, and artwork to join the room.

One thing we wouldn't do is fill the crib with decorative pillows, blankets, or stuffed animals. Those might look lovely in styled photos, but they don't belong in an infant's sleep space.

The Design Trick We'd Use: Plan the Room Twice

Before ordering a single piece of furniture, we'd sketch two versions of the nursery.

The first would show the newborn setup. A crib, a dresser with a changing station, a comfortable place to sit, and practical storage for diapers, clothes, and feeding supplies.

The second would show the same room a few years later. The crib in an approved toddler configuration, the changing tray removed, and perhaps a small reading or play area where baby supplies once lived.

It's a simple exercise that can reveal whether the pieces you're considering will actually work as your child grows.

We'd measure doors, windows, closets, and drawer clearance before choosing the layout. For the toddler version, we'd check the converted crib's dimensions and instructions rather than assuming it will occupy exactly the same space.

If a particular piece doesn't have a useful role in the second version of the room, we'd question whether it needs to be purchased right away.

That doesn't mean every nursery purchase needs to last forever. It simply means giving furniture a little more thought before buying.

What We'd Prioritize Beyond the Aesthetic

As much as we love a beautiful nursery, the things that matter most aren't always the most photogenic.

For the crib, we'd begin with the correct mattress dimensions, a firm and flat sleep surface, and the manufacturer's current assembly instructions.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recommends placing infants on their backs to sleep and keeping pillows, loose blankets, bumpers, and stuffed animals out of the crib.

We'd also pay attention to the materials used to make the furniture. dadadababy's cribs are GREENGUARD Gold Certified, which means they meet independent standards for low chemical emissions.

That certification is particularly relevant when considering indoor air quality, although it doesn't replace structural safety requirements, proper assembly, or safe-sleep practices.

For the dresser, we'd confirm that the selected changing tray is compatible, follow its installation instructions, and secure the furniture against tipping.

Beautiful design and practical safety considerations can absolutely coexist. In fact, we think the most thoughtfully designed nurseries make room for both.

How We'd Make the Nursery Last Beyond the Baby Years

Our biggest goal for an Alex Cooper-inspired nursery wouldn't be to create something that looks perfect for one photograph.

It would be to create a room that still feels beautiful when the baby becomes a toddler.

That's why we'd focus on a few lasting pieces and let smaller details change over time.

The walnut crib could transition into its next approved configuration. The dresser could continue storing clothing, books, and everyday essentials. The walls could stay neutral while new artwork and accessories reflect the child's changing interests.

We'd also make sure to keep the crib's assembly instructions and compatible conversion-part information somewhere accessible. Planning to convert a crib later is only useful when the required parts are available and approved for the exact model.

And rather than treating certifications, materials, and convertibility as interchangeable promises, we'd check each separately. Solid wood tells you about construction. GREENGUARD Gold addresses chemical emissions. Model-specific documentation tells you which conversions are supported.

It's these small decisions that help turn a nursery from a temporary setup into a room that grows with your family.

So, Would Alex Cooper Approve?

We can't say what Alex would actually choose for her baby's room. But if we were handed the creative brief, we'd aim for something that balances two sides of her public aesthetic: confident personality and understated comfort.

A beautiful walnut crib. Warm neutrals. A few unexpected details. Storage that works as hard as it looks good. And furniture that doesn't need replacing every time a new childhood milestone arrives.

Most importantly, it wouldn't be a nursery designed just to impress people.

It would be a room designed to be lived in, loved, and adapted as life changes.

And whether your style feels more like a celebrity home tour or a cozy corner you've put together yourself, that's a design philosophy we can all borrow.
